answer.rationale: The binding constraints are the 14-day expiry, no auto-renew, and a line at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer. That combination effectively rules out switch_primary_vendor this cycle: memory_c2 records a favorable switch, but nothing in it says the switch happened under a two-week clock with no inventory cushion, so its cost win cannot be transplanted here without importing migration risk directly into the delivery-risk constraint I am told not to worsen. defer_decision is also out — memory_c5's deferral worked because the item was non-critical and continued month-to-month; here the contract lapses outright on a critical primary line. add_second_source (memory_c3) is the right structural move but does not touch the 18% mandate and would consume the single available decision. That leaves negotiate_terms as the only lever that attacks cost without touching delivery continuity. The incumbent has refused to reopen price, but memory_c6 suggests a different door: term length and volume commitment unlocked pricing without narrowing scope — a structural change rather than a price reopening. So I am verifying memory_c6, because my whole plan rests on whether that volume-pricing win was genuinely driven by term length or was actually a repriced negotiation of the kind now foreclosed; if the archived record shows the latter, negotiate_terms collapses and renew_incumbent plus a bridge extension becomes the fallback. I am scoping this as a guarded move: pursue a short-dated commitment with volume flexibility and a bridge extension in hand, not a full multi-year lock. The downstream risk I want on record is that a long commitment bought for this year's 18% would freeze out both the low-cost vendor path from memory_c2 and the second-source resilience from memory_c3 for years, converting a one-cycle budget win into a durable loss of sourcing optionality. I also do not assume 18% is reachable through terms alone — it may not be, and the residual gap should surface at the next review rather than be papered over by an oversized commitment now.
